name: The Communist Manifesto
info: The Communist Manifesto is a political pamphlet written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels for the Communist League and published in London in 1848, setting out a view of history as a history of class struggles.

facts.made: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, commissioned by the Communist League; Engels is credited as co-author, but the final version was penned exclusively by Marx
facts.form: A pamphlet in German, 23 pages in its first printing, made up of a preamble and four sections; written over a span of 6 to 7 weeks
facts.where: Read in printed editions and translations in many languages; a manuscript page is held at the International Institute of Social History in Amsterdam
facts.known: The opening line about a spectre haunting Europe; the claim that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles; the closing call for workers to unite; the ten measures of its second section; the 1888 English edition translated by Samuel Moore

t: Marx and Engels wrote it for the Communist League, which commissioned it after its Second Congress of 1847; it appeared anonymously in London in late February 1848.
It describes history through modes of production and class struggle, argues that capitalism will bring about its own destruction, and predicts a revolution leading to a classless society.
After the defeat of the 1848 revolutions it fell into obscurity, then revived from the early 1870s and spread widely after the October Revolution of 1917.
dyk: Only one page of a draft of the Manifesto has ever been located. The historian Eric Hobsbawm takes the absence of any other preliminary drafts as evidence of haste, after the Communist League sent Marx an ultimatum demanding the manuscript by 1 February 1848.
ev: Engels writes the Draft of a Communist Confession of Faith for the League of the Just, then the Principles of Communism in October
The Second Congress of the League of Communists commissions Marx and Engels to draw up a manifesto
The Manifesto is published anonymously in London by the Communist Workers' Educational Association
George Julian Harney serialises Helen Macfarlane's translation in The Red Republican, the first English publication
Marx and Engels issue a new German edition, the first to carry the shortened title The Communist Manifesto
Samuel Moore's English translation, approved by Engels, appears and becomes the standard English edition
The first Chinese printing is distributed, funded by Grigori Voitinsky and translated by Chen Wangdao
A manuscript page is added to UNESCO's Memory of the World International Register

sections.origins:
The Manifesto came out of the League of the Just, which Marx and Engels joined in the spring of 1847 and which was soon convinced by their ideas of critical communism. At its First Congress, from 2 to 9 June, the League asked Engels to draft a creed setting out its programme. He wrote the Draft of a Communist Confession of Faith in question-and-answer form, like a catechism, with 22 questions and fairly terse answers. In October he found at the League's Paris branch, by then called the League of Communists, that Moses Hess had written a creed of his own. Engels criticised it severely, persuaded the rest of the League to entrust the task to him, and wrote the Principles of Communism, again as a catechism but with 25 questions and more detailed answers.

On 23 November, before the Second Congress, Engels wrote to Marx that he wished to drop the catechism format for a manifesto, which he felt must contain a certain amount of history. The Congress met from 29 November to 8 December 1847 at the headquarters of the German Workers' Education Association in Soho, London. After ten days of debate Marx, in Harold Laski's words, overcame stiff and prolonged opposition and won a majority for his programme. The League adopted a more combative resolution than in June and commissioned Marx, especially, and Engels to draw up a manifesto.
sections.content:
The Manifesto has a preamble and four sections. The preamble opens with the spectre of communism haunting Europe and notes that politicians in government and in opposition alike labelled their opponents communists; the authors infer that those in power treated communism as a power in itself, and they call on communists to publish their views and aims openly. The first section, Bourgeois and Proletarians, sets out historical materialism: the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. The authors argue that the bourgeoisie, the owners of the means of production, had by 1848 displaced the old powers of feudalism, and that in exploiting the proletariat it served as its own grave-diggers, since proletarians would become conscious of their potential and overthrow it.

The second section, Proletarians and Communists, describes the communists' relation to the rest of the working class and answers objections, such as that communism would abolish private property, advocate communal prostitution or discourage work. It ends with a list of short-term measures, including a progressive income tax, abolition of child labour, free public education and nationalisation of transport and communication. The third section separates communism from other socialist doctrines, such as Reactionary Socialism and Critical-Utopian Socialism and Communism. The fourth discusses the communist position towards opposition parties in France, Switzerland, Poland and Germany, and closes with a call for the working men of all countries to unite.
sections.making:
After the Second Congress Marx returned to Brussels, where, according to his biographer Francis Wheen, he engaged in ceaseless procrastination. He worked only intermittently on the Manifesto, lecturing on political economy at the German Workers' Education Association, writing for the Deutsche-Brüsseler-Zeitung and giving a long speech on free trade, and from 17 to 26 January 1848 he was in Ghent to set up a branch of the Democratic Association. Having heard nothing from him for nearly two months, the Central Committee of the Communist League sent an ultimatum on 24 or 26 January demanding the completed manuscript by 1 February. This pressure spurred Marx on, and he seems to have rushed to finish. Hobsbawm points to the absence of any extant preliminary drafts as evidence of the haste.

The whole text took 6 to 7 weeks. Engels is credited as co-author, but the final version was penned exclusively by Marx. Engels wrote in his preface to the 1883 German edition that the basic thought of the Manifesto belongs solely and exclusively to Marx. Laski does not disagree, though he suggests that Engels underplayed his own part and notes the close resemblance between its substance and the Principles of Communism. Anthony Arnove likewise holds that the kernel of the Manifesto is in the Principles of Communism and that Marx's task was to turn the catechism into a manifesto with more historical narrative and greater rhetorical force.
sections.reception:
The Manifesto appeared anonymously in late February 1848, issued by the Communist Workers' Educational Association at 46 Liverpool Street in London. It was a 23-page pamphlet in German with a dark-green cover, reprinted three times and serialised in the Deutsche Londoner Zeitung. Its preamble announced publication in English, French, German, Italian, Flemish and Danish, but the first printings were in German only. Its influence in the Europe-wide revolutions of 1848 was limited to Germany, where the Cologne-based Communist League and its Neue Rheinische Zeitung, edited by Marx, played a part. The newspaper was suppressed in May 1849, and in 1852 members of the League's central board were sentenced at Cologne to between three and six years in prison.

After the defeat of the revolutions the Manifesto fell into obscurity through the 1850s and 1860s. It revived in the early 1870s, which Hobsbawm attributes to three causes: Marx's leadership of the First International, his support for the Paris Commune of 1871, and the treason trial of leaders of the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Germany, at which prosecutors read the text into the court record, so that it could legally be published in Germany. Between 1871 and 1873 it appeared in over nine editions in six languages. The mass social-democratic parties did not require their members to know theory, and Hobsbawm notes that the Manifesto was read chiefly by party theoreticians, while small militant parties took pride in knowing it by heart.
sections.survival:
The text came down in printed editions, many of them revised by its authors. The version corrected for printing and punctuation mistakes in April and May 1848, at 30 pages, served as the basis for later editions. The German edition of 1872 carried a preface in which Marx and Engels said that some details had become dated after a quarter of a century, specifically the measures proposed in the second section, but that the general principles were on the whole as correct as ever. It was the first edition with the shortened title, and later editions were based on it. For the Russian edition of 1882, translated by Georgi Plekhanov, they wrote a new preface asking whether Russia could become communist directly or would become capitalist first. After Marx's death in March 1883 Engels wrote the prefaces to five editions between 1888 and 1893.

The first English publication was in November 1850, when George Julian Harney serialised Helen Macfarlane's translation in his Chartist newspaper The Red Republican, and his introduction revealed the authors' names for the first time. Her version began: A frightful hobgoblin stalks throughout Europe. The standard English edition is Samuel Moore's of 1888, approved by Engels, who added notes. A manuscript page of the Manifesto was added in 2013 to UNESCO's Memory of the World International Register, with Marx's annotated copy of Capital, Volume I; they are held among Marx's papers at the International Institute of Social History in Amsterdam.
sections.legacy:
After the October Revolution of 1917 the Soviet Union, a one-party state under the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, was founded explicitly along Marxist lines. The CPSU and the Leninist parties of the Third International expected their members to know the classic works of Marx, Engels and Lenin, so the Manifesto became required reading, and spreading these works became a policy objective, backed by a state's resources. In 1932 the American and British Communist Parties printed several hundred thousand copies of a cheap edition, probably the largest mass edition ever issued in English. In 1920 it was printed in Chinese, a priority of the Shanghai Communist Group, with Chen Wangdao credited as translator of the first printing, and it was dubbed the first red book of China. By its centenary in 1948 general publishers were printing it too, and Hobsbawm called it a political classic tout court.

Writers have judged it differently. Peter Osborne called it the single most influential text written in the nineteenth century. Critics such as Eduard Bernstein opposed the early Marxism it represented and held that the homogeneous working class it posited did not exist and that the middle class was growing. Seymour Lipset wrote in 1981 that its fundamental premise had been refuted by history, and Cory Doctorow called the imminent downfall of capitalism its most glaring defect. Hal Draper replied to Bernstein that the Manifesto itself says the middle class limps on in a more and more ruined state.

summary: The Communist Manifesto is a pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, commissioned by the Communist League and published in London in 1848. It describes history as class struggle and predicts a communist revolution. Obscure after 1848, it spread widely from the 1870s and after 1917.
references: Hal Draper, The Adventures of the Communist Manifesto (Haymarket Books, 2020)
Phil Gasper (ed.), The Communist Manifesto: A Road Map to History's Most Important Political Document (Haymarket Books, 2005)
David Black, Helen Macfarlane: A Feminist, Revolutionary Journalist, and Philosopher in Mid-nineteenth-century England (Lexington Books, 2004)
notes: The article says Marx's ultimatum came on 24 or 26 January; both given.

Left out: the article's sales estimate and its 'best-selling books' ranking, the 150th-anniversary editions and the shop-window anecdote, and commentary on Derrida, Milton and Shakespeare as influences.
Left out: the 'idiocy of rural life' passage and Dorschel's four concepts of change, to keep within length; the editor may add them.
The article gives Marx's date of death only as March 1883. The Manifesto's own preamble is quoted by the article as 'A spectre is haunting Europe', paraphrased here.

The article says the 'ten measures' were declared inapplicable to the present situation in the 1872 preface; the survival section renders this as 'some details had become dated, specifically the measures'.
